Baltimore City bus reliability

Scheduled MTA local bus stop events ·

Project C claim

Maryland law requires MTA to provide fare-free transit for eligible Baltimore City public school students for covered activities. The project asks how dependable that service is during school commute hours. The figures describe stop events across the public bus network. They do not measure the share of eligible students whose school trips were disrupted. Md. Code Ann., Transp. § 7–710(a)–(c)

The comparison uses Census tracts to measure poverty and vehicle access. The map below reports service by named neighborhood. Household vehicle access is an indicator of transportation options. The records cannot identify which students rode the bus or whether they arrived at school late.

Citywide service

Each record is one scheduled stop on one bus trip within Baltimore City. A trip can contribute several stop events.

How to read the citywide numbers
Canceled or more than 7 minutes late
The share of classified stop events with either outcome. A cancellation counts when the real-time feed flagged the trip as canceled and the tracker found no matching vehicle position.
On time among classified events
The share within two minutes early through seven minutes late. The denominator includes all timing classifications and classified cancellations.
Average vs. schedule
Add up the estimated timing differences and divide by the number of events with usable timing estimates. For example, an average of 4 min late means the measured stop events were four minutes behind schedule on average. Early times reduce the average. Cancellations and missing timings have no minute value and are excluded. The measure describes schedule adherence. Rider wait times are unknown.
Median vs. schedule
The middle timing difference when measured events are ordered from earliest to latest. It is less affected by a few unusually long delays.
Monitoring coverage
The share of scheduled stop events that fell within the tracker’s monitoring coverage. Some monitored events still lack a usable timing classification.
Classified events
The count of stop events classified as early, on time, late, very late, or canceled. Missing vehicle records, feed-flagged skips, and unclassified timing are shown separately in the counts below the cards.

What bus reliability means for students

Baltimore City Public Schools and MTA provide eligible students free public transit, including local bus service. For a student who depends on that bus, an early departure can mean waiting for the next one. A late or canceled bus can cause a missed connection and leave too little time to get to class. That risk matters especially when a student has few alternatives. The tracker measures service at stops during school commute hours. It does not record who boarded, whether students missed connections, or how much class time they lost.

City Schools’ 2026–27 student transit program · MTA student fares and eligibility · The Baltimore Banner’s school-commute analysis

What MTA and City Schools are responsible for

Maryland’s Transportation Article, § 7–710(a)–(c), requires MTA to provide fare-free transit to eligible Baltimore City public school students for school-related or educational extracurricular activities between 5 a.m. and 8 p.m. Under subsection (d), MTA must work with Baltimore City Public Schools and the Mayor’s Office of Employment Development to adopt eligibility regulations for the student and YouthWorks transit-pass programs. Maryland’s student transportation regulations separately make the local school system responsible for the safe operation of its student transportation system.

Section 7–710 requires access to covered transit from 5 a.m. to 8 p.m. It sets no punctuality, trip-completion, or arrival-at-school benchmark. The tracker samples the 6–9:30 a.m. and 2–5:30 p.m. commute windows. It cannot determine how consistently MTA provided access throughout the full statutory period.

The Baltimore Regional Transit Commission’s 2025 annual report describes an agreement under which MTA provides adjusted public bus service to accommodate students. The tracker’s citywide figures include general local bus stops and do not isolate service covered by that agreement. Assessing compliance would require the agreement and applicable rules, service records for affected routes, and evidence of what students experienced.

Md. Code Ann., Transp. § 7–710 · COMAR 11.06.05, Baltimore City student transit · COMAR 13A.06.07.03, student transportation · Baltimore Regional Transit Commission, 2025 annual report

What should count as reliable for a school trip?

MTA counts a local bus as on time within a window of two minutes early to seven minutes late. A bus can meet that benchmark and still arrive too late for a student’s transfer or first bell. The tracker uses the same tolerance for its own stop-event estimates. The citywide cards describe that sample and use different coverage and classification rules from MTA’s published performance series.

MeasureWhat it would tell us
On-time stop eventsHow often service falls within the schedule tolerance. Report coverage alongside the rate so readers can see how much service was observed.
Cancellations and early departuresHow often a planned boarding opportunity may be lost. Track confirmed cancellations and early departures separately from missing vehicle records.
Long waits and missed connectionsHow often students have to wait much longer than planned, and how much time they need to leave for transfers. Measuring this requires trip-level data.
Arrival before the first bellWhat share of observed school trips arrive before the school’s actual start time, and how many minutes of instruction are missed when they do not. Measuring this requires student-trip or attendance evidence.

What MTA and City Schools could report

  • MTA service delivery. On routes and trips that serve schools, report how many scheduled trips operated, how many were canceled, and how often buses left key boarding stops early. Show missing records separately and include the number of scheduled trips behind each rate.
  • Student access to instruction. City Schools and MTA could track how often sampled school journeys reach the school before the bell, how much extra time students need for a dependable trip, and which disruptions cause missed connections or class time. Report results by school and route using aggregate records.

These are proposed accountability measures. MTA’s schedule tolerance helps assess bus operations. Arrival before the bell tells us whether the full trip worked for students.

How to read the numbers

The map counts stops inside Baltimore City, including city stops on routes that cross the city line. Classified events include timing estimates and eligible feed-flagged cancellations. Missing vehicle records can reflect a missed trip or a tracking gap. A single bus trip can contribute several stop events.

Citywide totals include city stops that could not be assigned to a single neighborhood.

Neighborhood demographics. The 2020–2024 American Community Survey estimates are fixed across commute views. Neighborhood figures are approximate: we allocate each tract’s counts by the share of its area overlapping the neighborhood, sum the estimated counts, and divide by the estimated population or household total. This assumes people and households are evenly distributed within each tract. The project’s claim was tested using the original Census tract rates.
